_comment: Permission profile for VOICE-originated sessions (HIMMEL-1522).
voice-policy.json marks two rules `hard: true` — off the evolution path,
not reachable by any growth in trust: `secrets` and `policy-edit`. It also
denies `salus`. `--permission-mode plan` enforces none of those: it blocks
WRITES, while all three are about READS. A spoken request could still have
a credential or a medical record read out loud, which is precisely the
hazard the policy names — the exposure is the ROOM and anything recording
in it, not the person asking.
So the deny rules below are the structural half of that policy. plan mode
covers writes; this covers reads. Passed via --settings on every voice
spawn, which is the highest non-managed precedence, so it cannot be
widened by a prompt — and voice cannot edit this file either, because
`policy-edit` is denied and plan mode blocks the write.
PATTERN SYNTAX — `//` IS REQUIRED, and this was verified by running it,
not by reading it. Round 5 removed a `//` prefix on the reasoning that it
appears nowhere in this repo's own working rules. That reasoning was
backwards, and it made this entire file inert outside the working
directory. A bare `Read(**/x)` is resolved RELATIVE TO THE PROJECT ROOT,
so it only ever covered files under the himmel checkout. The real salus
vault, ~/.ssh, ~/.aws and every ~/.env live OUTSIDE that tree and were
matched by nothing. `//` anchors the pattern at the filesystem root, which
is the whole point here: this profile has to protect paths the repo does
not contain.
Observed directly (same file, same rules, only cwd changed):
cwd = the file's own tree   -> `File is in a directory that is denied`
cwd = the himmel repo root  -> read SUCCEEDED, no block
and with `//` restored, the same outside-cwd read is refused. The repo's
own rules omit `//` correctly — they guard in-repo paths, where relative
is what you want. This file is the opposite case.
ONLY `Read(...)` RULES FUNCTION HERE. Also measured, not assumed:
- a lone `Read(//**/salus/**)` blocks the Grep tool too, so Read rules
cover every file-reading tool and per-tool duplicates buy nothing;
- `Glob(...)` rules are rejected — the harness prints a warning per rule
on every single voice turn saying they are not matched by file
permission checks;
- `Grep(...)` rules are worse: SILENTLY inert. A profile carrying only
`Grep(//**/salus/**)` let the Grep through with no warning at all.
The 13 Grep and 8 Glob entries this file used to carry were therefore
pure decoration. They are gone rather than left in as reassurance.
THIS FILE CANNOT REACH MCP TOOLS — the launchers close that, not these
rules (CR round 6, [codex-adv-1]). A permission rule names a TOOL, and an
MCP tool's name is chosen by its server (`mcp__tokensave__tokensave_read`
and friends), so no pattern here can ever cover one. Probed on a real voice
spawn: that reader was available and entirely outside this deny tier. Both
launchers now pass `--strict-mcp-config` with NO `--mcp-config`, which
resolves to zero MCP servers. If you ever add an `--mcp-config` to a voice
launcher you re-open this hole, and nothing in THIS file will warn you.
`.claude.json` was missing from the secrets list (CR round 6,
[codex-adv-2]) — it holds MCP server specs including API keys, on a profile
claiming to enforce the policy's HARD `secrets` rule. Added, along with the
other common token stores.
AND THIS IS STILL A DENY-LIST — the honest caveat, and the reason this file
does NOT yet deliver the policy's HARD `secrets` guarantee. Round 4
concluded a deny-list over ways to READ cannot be completed, and denied Bash
outright to terminate that regress. The conclusion was right; the scope was
too narrow. Round 6 found three more entries (MCP tools, `.claude.json`, and
session resume — which is not a file read at all). Round 7 found two more
(`.config/gcloud`, `.azure`, then `.codex/auth.json`, `gh/hosts.yml`). Every
one is genuinely fixed above; the LIST is what keeps failing, because it
enumerates what to refuse from an open-ended set. Adding entry N+1 is not
convergence, it is the same move that produced entries 1..N.
The fix is to invert the polarity — an allow-list of readable roots behind a
broker, where a missing entry costs a refused read the operator NOTICES,
rather than a silent disclosure nobody notices. That is HIMMEL-1549, and it
is not something this file can do. Until it lands, read the guarantee here
as best-effort, not as the policy's HARD rule.
THE SESSION-TRANSCRIPT STORE IS THE ONE TO NOTICE (CR round 9). Round 6
gave the loop its own session id so voice could not `--resume` the
operator's typed session. That closed the RESUME path and left the FILE
path wide open: `~/.claude/projects/**` holds every typed session as JSONL
— prompts, replies, tool output — and Read reached it. Probed: the read
succeeded. Denied now, along with the voice loop log. Worth stating plainly
because it is the same lesson twice: isolating a mechanism does not isolate
the DATA that mechanism wrote to disk.
POWERSHELL IS DENIED TOO — and the reason is not the one first proposed.
The round-9 finding claimed PowerShell bypasses every read-side deny. That
specific claim is FALSE and was disproved by probe: `Get-Content` on a
`.env` INSIDE the working directory is refused, so the Read rules do reach
the PowerShell tool's file access (paths outside the cwd are refused
earlier still, by working-directory scoping). It is denied anyway, for the
reason Bash is: it is a full shell. Plan mode blocks writes, not
`Invoke-WebRequest`, so leaving it enabled keeps an egress path open on an
unauthenticated channel — and denying Bash while allowing PowerShell is
incoherent on a Windows-primary machine. Enumerating safe PowerShell verbs
is the same non-terminating exercise that denying Bash outright ended.
WHY BASH IS DENIED OUTRIGHT, not pattern-matched. Successive review rounds
kept finding another way through: cat was blocked, so head/less/tail/more
were not; block those and awk, sed, python -c, Get-Content remain. A
deny-list over ways to read a file cannot be completed — every round adds
one more entry and the guarantee never actually arrives. Denying the tool
terminates that, and it is the honest posture for a channel that cannot
authenticate its speaker.
The cost is real and deliberate: voice cannot check CI, run git status, or
shell out at all. Restoring a narrow ALLOW-list of safe read-only commands
is HIMMEL-1536; an allow-list is completable where a deny-list is not.
Full enforcement of the CONFIRM tier still needs an action classifier
(HIMMEL-1535). This file closes the DENY tier only.
